name: Error & ignorance
who: Plato; Aquinas; most of the rationalist tradition
implies: Inquiry, refutation, instruction.
summary: Two contradictory claims cannot both be true, so at least one party is wrong. On this view, disagreement is a symptom of error, and error is a lack of knowledge. Socratic intellectualism adds that no one errs willingly. Correct the belief and the dispute dissolves. Most people assume this account without stating it.

name: Inconsistency & aporia
implies: Elenchus, obligational games, commitment-tracking.
summary: The disagreement that matters is within a person, among beliefs they already hold. An interlocutor is shown that their commitments cannot all stand. The external opponent is only the occasion for internal disagreement. Formal dialectic later makes this precise as a commitment store that has to stay consistent.

name: Disputed reputable opinion
implies: Dialectic, rhetoric, the method of endoxa (Nicomachean Ethics VII.1).
summary: Some questions belong to things that ‘admit of being otherwise’, where only probable premises are available. Reputable opinions conflict, and working through the puzzles (diaporēsai) on both sides is how one approaches first principles. On this view, disagreement is the normal state of practical and dialectical reasoning, and nobody need have blundered.

name: Partial perspectives
who: Protagoras; Jain logicians; J. S. Mill; Nietzsche
implies: Standpoint indexing, both-sides argument, synthesis.
summary: Each party sees a real aspect of something larger. The blind men are each right about the elephant and wrong only in saying ‘only’. Mill’s secular version holds that conflicting doctrines ‘share the truth between them’. Nietzsche’s holds that ‘there is only a perspective seeing’, and that the more eyes we bring to a thing, the more complete our ‘objectivity’.

name: Undecidability
implies: Suspension; critique of the question; demarcation.
summary: Some disputes are interminable because the arguments on each side are of equal force (isostheneia). For Sextus this is a reason to suspend judgment. For Kant, the antinomies show reason in conflict with itself whenever it overreaches experience. The deadlock comes from the question, so neither disputant is at fault.

name: Calculation error
implies: Formalisation; ‘Calculemus!’
summary: With an adequate notation, every dispute would be a mistake in calculation, checkable like a sum. On this view, people disagree because natural language is imprecise.

name: Unfinished inquiry
implies: Better experiments; patience; fallibilism.
summary: On this view, a community disagrees because its inquiry has not yet converged. Under the method of science, the opinion ‘fated to be ultimately agreed to by all who investigate’ is what we mean by truth. Disagreement is a stage that inquiry will pass through.

name: Burdens of judgment
implies: Toleration; public reason; deliberation without expectation of convergence.
summary: Reasonable people disagree without any of them being irrational or ill-willed. Evidence is complex and conflicting. People weigh considerations differently. Concepts are vague at the edges. Total life experience shapes judgment. Normative considerations pull both ways, and every institution must select among values. Rawls calls reasonable pluralism the normal result of human reason exercised under free institutions.

name: Divergent priors & models
who: Robert Aumann; Robin Hanson; Tyler Cowen; CFAR
implies: Share evidence; locate cruxes; bet; update.
summary: Bayesian agents with common priors whose posteriors are common knowledge cannot agree to disagree. Persistent disagreement implies different priors, private information that has not been shared, or something other than honest truth-seeking. Cowen and Hanson conclude that most disagreements are dishonest, because each party gives its own judgment more weight than it should. The practical version breaks the dispute down into world-models and finds the crux.

name: Higher-order evidence
who: Thomas Kelly; David Christensen; Adam Elga
implies: Calibrated humility; or principled steadfastness.
summary: Suppose you learn that an epistemic peer, someone as informed and as able as you, disagrees with you. Epistemologists ask whether you should then move toward their view. Conciliationists (Christensen, Elga) say yes: ‘equal weight’. Steadfast views (Kelly) say the first-order evidence still counts. On this view, the disagreement counts as evidence, including evidence about your own reliability.

name: Incommensurable paradigms
implies: Translation, exemplars and time. No crucial experiment will settle it.
summary: Across a revolution, scientists ‘practice their trades in different worlds’. They disagree about which problems matter, what counts as a solution and what terms mean, so that there is no neutral algorithm of choice. Persuasion across paradigms resembles conversion.

name: Disorder of names
implies: Rectify names, by sage convention or by disputation.
summary: Disputes arise when names no longer track realities and roles. For the Mohists, every bian is about whether a name fits. For Xunzi, deviant sophists who ‘confuse names’ create disorder that a true king must correct.

name: Equivocation & verbal dispute
who: Aristotle; Peter Abelard; William James; David Chalmers
implies: Distinguo; taboo the word; restate without the term.
summary: The parties use one word in two senses and so do not contradict each other. Aristotle classes homonymy first among the fallacies dependent on language. Abelard reconciles authorities by distinguishing senses. In James’s squirrel case, whether a man ‘goes round’ a squirrel depends on what ‘round’ means. Chalmers proposes the ‘method of elimination’: ban the contested word and see whether a dispute remains.

name: Disagreement in attitude
implies: Separate belief from attitude; treat persuasive definitions as moves in the argument.
summary: Stevenson distinguishes disagreement in belief, about how things are, from disagreement in attitude, about what to favour. Ethical disputes are chiefly the latter, carried on in language that sounds descriptive. Belief-change can shift attitude, but nothing guarantees it will.

name: Metalinguistic negotiation
implies: Make the normative question about usage explicit (conceptual engineering).
summary: Many apparently factual disputes, such as whether Secretariat is an ‘athlete’ or whether waterboarding is ‘torture’, are disputes about how a word ought to be used. These disputes are real and important because words have practical consequences. So a dispute about words can matter as much as a dispute about facts.

name: Hinges & language-games
implies: Show the practice instead of proving; expect conversion; describe the other’s game patiently.
summary: Some propositions are hinges on which doubting turns. No argument established them. When two parties’ hinges differ, reasons run out. ‘Where two principles really do meet which cannot be reconciled with one another, then each man declares the other a fool and heretic.’ ‘At the end of reasons comes persuasion.’

name: Clash of final vocabularies
implies: Redescription; irony; keep the conversation going.
summary: Everyone carries a ‘final vocabulary’, words beyond which they have only circular argument. Evidence cannot settle a dispute between vocabularies. One side redescribes the other’s vocabulary in its own terms, or the conversation continues. Rorty’s edifying philosophy aims to keep the conversation going and makes no attempt to end it with truth.

name: The differend
implies: Bear witness; find idioms for what cannot yet be phrased.
summary: A differend is a conflict between parties that cannot be equitably resolved because no rule of judgment applies to both. To settle it in one party’s idiom wrongs the other, whose harm cannot be stated in that idiom. Litigation presupposes a shared genre. In a differend there is none.

name: Contested validity claims
implies: Discourse; ideal speech situation.
summary: Speech acts implicitly claim truth, rightness and sincerity. Disagreement occurs when a hearer rejects one of these claims. The rejected claim shows which kind of argument is needed: theoretical discourse for truth, practical discourse for rightness, and consistent conduct over time for sincerity.

name: What cannot be measured
implies: Find a measure, or accept enduring enmity.
summary: Socrates observes that disputes about number, size and weight are ended by counting, measuring and weighing. The disputes that cause anger and enmity concern the just and unjust, the noble and shameful, the good and bad, for which we have no agreed standard of decision. It is the earliest explicit statement that value disagreements differ in kind.

name: Value pluralism
implies: Choose and own the choice; build institutions for coexistence.
summary: The ultimate values of life are irreconcilable. ‘The various value spheres of the world stand in irreconcilable conflict with each other.’ Berlin adds that goods are many and cannot be measured on one scale. They conflict, so every choice entails a tragic loss. On this view, disagreement can be accurate: the parties correctly see that their values are incompatible.

name: Moral foundations
implies: Moral reframing; humility about one’s own foundations.
summary: Moral judgment rests on a few intuitive foundations: care, fairness, loyalty, authority, sanctity and, later, liberty. Political camps weight these differently. Reasoning mostly follows intuition, like a rider on an elephant, so disputes conducted in one camp’s foundations do not land in the other’s.

name: Sacred values
who: Philip Tetlock; Scott Atran; Robert Axelrod
implies: Symbolic concessions; reframing; never price the sacred.
summary: Some values are protected from trade-offs, and offering money for them provokes moral outrage. Rational-choice bargaining backfires here. Symbolic gestures such as apology or recognition can open paths that material concessions close. Much conflict that looks like a clash of interests is a misdiagnosed clash of sacred values.

name: Interests beneath positions
who: Mary Parker Follett; Roger Fisher; William Ury
implies: Ask why; invent options; integrative bargaining.
summary: What people say they want, their positions, is a strategy for what they need, their interests. Positions are often incompatible where the interests behind them are not. Disagreement is about allocation, and allocation is a design problem.

name: Faction & party
implies: Institutional design that multiplies and balances factions.
summary: Hume sorts real factions into those from interest, those from principle (‘abstract speculative principle’, which he finds peculiar to modern times) and those from affection. Madison: the ‘latent causes of faction are thus sown in the nature of man’, and ‘the most common and durable source’ is the unequal distribution of property. These causes cannot be removed, so their effects must be controlled by an extended republic.

name: Mixed-motive game
implies: Bargaining analysis; credible commitments; focal points.
summary: Schelling holds that few conflicts are pure. The parties have a common interest in avoiding mutual loss and a conflicting interest over how to divide gains. What looks like argument is often signalling, commitment and the search for a focal point.

name: Class interest & ideology
implies: Ideology critique; organising; changing the material base.
summary: ‘The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.’ Ideas follow material positions, and the ruling ideas are the ideas of the ruling class. Many intellectual disagreements are class antagonisms in disguise.

name: Contest & honour
who: Greek agonistic culture; the sophists; Schopenhauer
implies: Rules, judges, audiences; or withdrawal from the arena.
summary: Argument is a form of combat whose stake is standing. The contest is good in itself as an arena of excellence (Hesiod’s ‘good Eris’). In its degenerate form it is vanity defended by any means. What is at issue is who prevails before an audience, and the proposition matters less.

name: War & sovereignty
implies: Arbitration; delegation of judgment.
summary: Private judgment about right and wrong is the seed of civil war. Hobbes treats dispute as a condition that precedes politics and that only a sovereign arbiter can end. ‘Right reason’ is whatever reason the parties have agreed to treat as authoritative.

name: Friend & enemy
implies: Decision, not debate (Schmitt); or agonistic taming (Mouffe).
summary: The specifically political distinction is between friend and enemy. Any opposition, whether religious, moral or economic, becomes political when it is intense enough to group people as friends and enemies. Liberal discussion hopes to dissolve the political into endless conversation and therefore misunderstands it.

name: Hegemony
implies: Agonistic institutions; counter-hegemonic struggle.
summary: Every social order is a contingent hegemonic articulation, and every consensus excludes. Disagreement marks what the current settlement suppresses. Mouffe’s aim is to give it legitimate expression.

name: Power / knowledge
implies: Genealogy; problematisation; attention to who is authorised to speak.
summary: Each society has its ‘regime of truth’, which governs the types of discourse it accepts as true and who is authorised to say what counts. Disputes over truth are also struggles over the rules that produce truth. Who may speak is decided before what is said.

name: Vanity & obstinacy
who: Schopenhauer; Montaigne; the Buddha of Sn 4
implies: Lower the stakes of being wrong; or exploit them (eristic).
summary: Most people cannot bear to be shown wrong. Once a position is stated, defending it becomes a matter of self-regard, and the original question is abandoned. Montaigne thought obstinacy and heat of opinion the surest sign of a weak mind.

name: Unmet needs
implies: Needs-based dialogue; ‘provention’ (Burton’s coinage).
summary: Beneath interests lie universal human needs: security, identity, recognition, autonomy, meaning. Needs cannot be bargained over, but they can be satisfied, and they seldom conflict. Conflict is what unmet needs sound like.

name: Threat & defensiveness
implies: Restate before rebutting; reduce threat; evoke instead of arguing.
summary: A person who feels threatened cannot hear. Evaluation is experienced as threat, and threat produces rigidity. Many disagreements persist because each side’s argument raises the other’s defences. The obstacle is emotional, so better logic cannot remove it.

name: Narcissism of small differences
implies: Notice how close the opponent is.
summary: Communities with adjoining territories, and those related to each other in other ways, are especially prone to feud and ridicule. Hostility is greatest between those who are nearly alike. Disagreement here does not track distance of views. It serves the group’s cohesion and its narcissism.

name: Mimetic rivalry
implies: Recognise the double; refuse the scapegoat.
summary: We desire what the model desires, so imitation makes rivals of those who are alike. As rivalry escalates, the object disappears and the rivals become doubles, each mirroring the other’s violence. Communities resolve the crisis by uniting against a scapegoat.

name: Argumentative reasoning
who: Hugo Mercier; Dan Sperber; Dan Kahan
implies: Argue in groups with real diversity; decouple facts from identity.
summary: Reasoning evolved for social exchange, where people produce arguments and evaluate the arguments of others. Individuals show myside bias when producing arguments and are better at judging others’ arguments. Groups that argue can outperform individuals. Kahan adds identity-protective cognition: partisans who are better with numbers polarise more on politicised facts.

name: Developmental form
implies: Hold your system as object; ask what each frame is for.
summary: The same disagreement takes a different shape depending on how a person makes meaning. At a ‘self-authoring’ order, one is one’s ideology and conflict is between systems. At a ‘self-transforming’ order, one can hold one’s own system as object, so conflict becomes a sign of over-identification with a partial form. Chapman’s ‘meta-rationality’ treats the fit between frame and situation as the real question.

name: Identity
who: Henri Tajfel; John Turner; Douglas Stone
implies: Decouple claim from identity; affirm before challenging.
summary: People derive self-esteem from group membership, and intergroup comparison drives conflict even over trivial distinctions (the minimal-group paradigm). In dyads, the ‘identity conversation’ asks what being wrong would say about me. Conceding the point feels like losing oneself.

name: Struggle for recognition
who: G. W. F. Hegel; Axel Honneth
implies: Recognition as remedy; attend to disrespect beneath the stated grievance.
summary: Self-consciousness exists only in being acknowledged, so the first conflict is a life-and-death struggle for recognition. Honneth turns this into a moral grammar of social conflict. Disrespect in love, rights and esteem drives struggles that appear to be about other things.

name: Relationship-level message
who: Paul Watzlawick; Janet Beavin Bavelas; Don Jackson
implies: Metacommunicate; change the pattern, not the topic.
summary: Every communication has a content aspect and a relationship aspect, and the latter classifies the former. Couples argue about the dishes while negotiating dominance and care. Each party also ‘punctuates’ the sequence differently (‘I withdraw because you nag’; ‘I nag because you withdraw’), so each sees the other as the cause.

name: Harm to relationship
who: Howard Zehr; restorative and indigenous traditions
implies: Repair; circles; reintegration.
summary: Restorative justice sees conflict and crime as wounds in a web of relationships. It replaces the questions ‘who is right?’ and ‘what rule was broken?’ with ‘who was hurt, and what do they need?’

name: Character & motive
implies: Purify motive; judge disputes by their spirit.
summary: Disagreement tests who you are. The Mishnah judges a dispute by whether it is ‘for the sake of Heaven’, and Socratic examination is examination of a life. The exchange is judged by the disputants’ intention and virtue more than by its outcome.

name: Affective polarisation
implies: Bridging ranking; cross-cutting contact; de-sorting.
summary: Partisans increasingly dislike and distrust each other, often more than their policy differences warrant. Disagreement now sorts people by social identity, and media ranked by engagement amplify the sorting. Researchers measure it as hostility between groups, which can grow while policy views stay close.

name: Attachment to views
implies: Non-dispute; emptiness of views; suspension.
summary: Suffering in dispute comes from grasping at views (diṭṭhi-upādāna). Which view is right matters less. Even right view, held as a possession, breeds conflict. The remedy is to let go of positions altogether.

name: ‘This’ and ‘that’
implies: Walking two roads; illumination.
summary: Every ‘this is so’ (shi) is made from a standpoint, and from the other side it is ‘that’ (bi). The Confucians and Mohists affirm what the other denies. The sage sees that ‘this’ and ‘that’ generate each other, and rests at the pivot from which both can be allowed.

name: Incomplete discernment
implies: Wait in silence; seek unity, not majority.
summary: Truth is one and is discerned together. Persisting disagreement means the gathered meeting has not yet waited long enough for the Light. A lone objector may be right, which is why a block is honoured.

name: Plurality willed from above
implies: Record minority views; decide without declaring falsehood.
summary: ‘These and these are the words of the living God.’ Contradictory rulings can both belong to revelation. Halakhic decision is necessary for practice, but the rejected opinion stays Torah, is studied, and may be revived. On this view, revelation unfolds through disagreement.

name: Disagreement as mercy
implies: Tolerate madhhab difference; study khilāf.
summary: Diverse rulings reached by sincere ijtihād are each rewarded, even when mistaken. A saying attributed to the Prophet, ‘the disagreement of my community is a mercy’, is weakly attested, yet it has been widely cited. Jurists read the plurality of the schools as latitude for believers.

name: Strife as engine
implies: Sharpen, then sublate, the contradiction.
summary: ‘War is father of all and king of all.’ ‘Justice is strife.’ Opposition is the motor of becoming. Hegel makes contradiction the self-movement of the concept, and Marx locates it in material relations. On this view, history and thought advance through disagreement.

name: Collision with error
implies: Free discussion; devil’s advocacy; protect dissent.
summary: Truth unchallenged becomes dead dogma. Even a false dissent is useful, because it forces the defenders of a truth to earn it again, and so to understand it.

name: Conflict as sociation
implies: Institutionalise conflict; encourage divisions that cut across one another.
summary: For Simmel, conflict is a form of social relation. It binds the antagonists, clarifies boundaries, and creates group cohesion. Cross-cutting conflicts can stitch a society together.

name: Constructive difference
implies: Integration over compromise.
summary: Follett asks us to think of conflict as friction in an engine. In itself it is neither good nor bad. It is the appearance of difference, and invention starts from difference. Integration produces something new that neither party brought.
